findings.headline: Council changed from Labour-led to a Green Party and Liberal Democrat coalition after the May 2026 elections
findings.detail: The paper says this report covers the position before the election. From May 2026 the Cabinet was renamed the Executive.
findings.matters: A change of controlling administration shortly after a year of reserve drawdown and a widening funding gap affects the Council's budget decisions from 2026/27.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: from being Labour-led to a coalition between the Green Party and Liberal Democrats

findings.headline: Residents expressed concern over 2025/26 about the reliability of service charge statements, particularly for district heating
findings.detail: The paper says the concern may be linked to gas prices affecting the heating costs borne by residents. The auditor says there is a risk residents may not trust the process, and recommends independent attestation of the statements, as other councils and large housing associations do.
findings.matters: Concern over service charge statements on district heating shows a recovery risk and a trust risk that other councils with leasehold charges face.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: There has been some concern by residents over the course of 2025/26 regarding the reliability of the service charge statements

findings.headline: 76% of Southwark 2030 Delivery Plan commitments (87 of 115) were delivered or on track at Q2 2025/26, against 80% at Q2 2024/25
findings.detail: The paper says 27 commitments were progressing but facing challenges or delays, and two were assessed as at risk. Areas needing focus included housing void turnaround times and recycling performance.
findings.matters: A fall in the share of delivery plan commitments on track, with housing voids among the named challenges, is the operational signal peer councils use to judge delivery capacity.
findings.figures: 87 of 115 commitments (76%) delivered or on track at Q2 2025/26; 80% at Q2 2024/25; 27 progressing with challenges or delays; 2 at risk
findings.quote: or 76%, were delivered or on track, compared with 80% at Q2 2024/25

findings.headline: Three largest counterparties accounted for approximately 75% of the Council's total spend with counterparties
findings.detail: The paper says these partnerships support the newbuild and refurbishment programmes, including British Land at Canada Water and NHG at Aylesbury. The auditor says the Council needs to manage the risk of a counterparty failing to proceed with its contribution.
findings.matters: Concentration of counterparty spend in three partners is a delivery and counterparty risk that finance directors and lenders assess when reviewing regeneration pipelines.
findings.figures: Approximately 75% of total spend with counterparties (three largest)
findings.quote: three largest counterparties represented approximately 75%

findings.headline: Aylesbury Estate delivery revised with NHG; responsibility for future phases 2C, 3 and 4 returns to the Council
findings.detail: NHG is expected to complete Phase 2B, FDS C and Plot 18. The auditor says the change creates a potential risk to the timing of the capital programme while the Council procures a new development partner. It also says this reduces dependence on a single partner.
findings.matters: A regeneration programme moving from a development partner back to the council changes the funding and timing exposure that lenders and peer councils assess on large schemes.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: responsibility for future phases 2C, 3 and 4 will return to the Council

findings.headline: Auditor records a recurring finding that the Council did not comply with the procurement rules in force at the time
findings.detail: The auditor recommends staff reminders and mechanisms to enforce and detect non-compliance. The auditor says it found no evidence of procurement breaches in 2025/26, but the Council must ensure rules are complied with on an ongoing basis.
findings.matters: A recurring procurement non-compliance finding, with no 2025/26 breaches found, is the position other councils will compare with their own contract controls.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: A recurring finding is that the Council did not comply with its procurement rules as were in force at the time.

findings.headline: Council's contract standing orders published in December 2025 add retrospective gateway approval for procurement started without prior approval
findings.detail: The paper says the revised standing orders explicitly distinguish exemptions from retrospective approvals. It describes this as a strengthening compared with the prior year, when the Council did not run a single central register of tender waivers.
findings.matters: A central register of tender waivers and a retrospective approval rule are procurement controls that finance directors check when assessing how waivers are governed.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: the council did not operate a single central register of tender waivers

findings.headline: Local Government Ombudsman upheld 46 of 48 complaints investigated, with key themes in housing and homelessness, and education and SEND
findings.detail: The paper compares this with 52 upheld complaints in 2024/25. It also reports 47 Housing Ombudsman cases of maladministration or severe maladministration, up from 42, mainly relating to responsive repairs and stakeholder relationships.
findings.matters: A high proportion of complaints upheld by the Ombudsman, with housing repairs among the themes, points to service failures that other councils and lenders will track.
findings.figures: 46 of 48 complaints upheld (2025/26); 52 upheld (2024/25); 47 Housing Ombudsman cases of maladministration or severe maladministration (2025/26); 42 (2024/25)
findings.quote: 46 of 48 complaints investigated were upheld

findings.headline: Auditor says its value for money work is not complete while it investigates an objection to the accounts
findings.detail: The auditor says that although it has reached its conclusions on significant value for money risks, the objection investigation may revise its value for money conclusion. The matters in the report may therefore change.
findings.matters: A value for money conclusion that is still open pending an objection is a live audit risk that a finance director and lender would monitor before relying on the report.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: we are investigating an objection to the accounts and this work may result in a revision to our value for money conclusion.

findings.headline: Auditor identified no significant weaknesses in the Council's value for money arrangements for 2025/26, after two significant weaknesses in 2024/25
findings.detail: The auditor reports no significant risks in financial sustainability and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Governance was assessed as having identified risks of significant weakness, but none was found to be an actual significant weakness. The direction of travel is marked as upwards for risks.
findings.matters: A move from two significant value for money weaknesses to none is the outcome a peer council or lender would compare against its own arrangements.
findings.figures: Two significant weaknesses identified in 2024/25; none identified in 2025/26
findings.quote: We identified no significant weaknesses in respect of the arrangements the Council has put in place

findings.headline: Auditor issued an unmodified opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements and on the Southwark Pension Fund financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor says the financial statements give a true and fair view. It identified no material misstatements in the key audit risk areas it covers, including dwelling valuation and pension liabilities. The Whole of Government Accounts work remained unconcluded at the time of the report.
findings.matters: An unmodified opinion with no material misstatement in the key areas is the baseline a lender checks before relying on the accounts.
findings.figures: Council dwellings valued over £3.6bn; no material misstatements identified
findings.quote: We issued an unmodified opinion on these financial statements.

findings.headline: Council says a further counter-fraud investigation into Devon Mansions and Consort Estate major works would not be proportionate
findings.detail: The auditor recommended a priority counter-fraud investigation because the Council had not established whether fraud occurred. The Council's management response says earlier review work gave reasonable assurance and that the historic records are limited. The paper names Consort Estate in this recommendation, whereas earlier text names Canada Estate.
findings.matters: A council declining an auditor's recommendation for a fraud investigation on major works contracts is a governance position that other councils and lenders will weigh.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: the Council does not consider that a further counter-fraud investigation would be proportionate or provide sufficient additional assurance.

findings.headline: Auditor is satisfied governance of the 2025/26 Consort Estate major works scheme has been strengthened, while noting the contract administrator and clerk of works are the same organisation
findings.detail: The auditor cites minutes, highlight reports, change orders and an in-house quantity surveyor as evidence of active monitoring. It says the auditor cannot guarantee the scheme will be delivered on budget. The auditor recommends segregating the contract administrator and clerk of works roles.
findings.matters: Evidence of tighter contract control on a live major works scheme, after the earlier Devon Mansions and Canada Estate failures, is what peer councils are assessing in their own programmes.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: As we could see evidence of the Council thoroughly challenging project progress, costs, and the work of its third party agents, we were satisfied that arrangements to manage the major works scheme have been strengthened.

findings.headline: Auditor says the Canada Estate major works scheme has reached practical completion, with Devon Mansions continuing
findings.detail: The paper says the Council is remediating historically poorly performed works at these schemes after resident lobbying and internal investigations. It says the Housing Scrutiny Commission monitors the remediation, and that some actions were closed without improvements being fully embedded.
findings.matters: Completion of a scheme that carried a prior significant weakness, with another still open, shows how far the remediation has progressed.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: with Canada Estate reaching practical completion (Devon Mansions is continuing).

findings.headline: Auditor reports the Council's stock condition survey has identified a decency rate in line with its peers
findings.detail: The auditor says this reduces the risk it identified last year of a significant financial outlay to make homes decent. It judges the related recommendation partially implemented, and says the Council has not yet fully reported to members the actions to ensure homes are decent. The paper cites the regulator's earlier finding that around 30% of homes did not meet the Decent Homes Standard.
findings.matters: A decency rate in line with peers, if confirmed by a complete survey, bears directly on the size of a housing capital backlog that a council and its lenders must fund.
findings.figures: Around 30% of homes not meeting the Decent Homes Standard (regulator's finding, prior year); last stock condition survey 2010 on a representative sample
findings.quote: has identified that its decency rate is high and in line with its peers

findings.headline: Council remains formally graded C3 by the Regulator of Social Housing following the November 2024 judgement
findings.detail: The paper says the Council continued to implement significant remedial actions during 2025/26. It also says the Council has not identified a material unexpected repair requirement from the first tranche of its stock condition survey.
findings.matters: A continuing C3 grade from the regulator, with remedial work under way, is a regulatory exposure that lenders to housing providers track.
findings.figures: Grade C3 (Consumer Standards)
findings.quote: The Council remains formally graded C3 by the Regulator of Social Housing

findings.headline: The HRA reserve rose by approximately £4m to £24.8m at year end, after a similar £4m increase in 2024/25
findings.detail: The paper calls the £25m reserve small for a Council of this size. It says the HRA is being rebuilt under a recovery plan, and that the Council is not yet in a position where the HRA is financially sustainable. The surplus came from cost control, disposal of uneconomic assets and higher income from charges.
findings.matters: A second year of HRA reserve growth under a recovery plan is the evidence a peer council or lender would look for before judging a housing revenue account as stabilising.
findings.figures: HRA reserve approximately £24.8m at 31 March 2026 (paper also refers to £25m); increase of approximately £4m in 2025/26 and £4m in 2024/25; actual HRA surplus £3,954k (2025/26) against £3,909k (2024/25)
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the HRA reserve increased by approximately £4 million to £24.8 million at year end

findings.headline: Year-end borrowings were £1,218,836k at 31 March 2026, against £1,168,786k a year earlier
findings.detail: The paper reports these figures in its key financial metrics table. It says the HRA is now borrowing to fund capital investment, and that the Council is likely to need to borrow for essential capital expenditure for some time.
findings.matters: Year-end borrowing growth of £50,050k in one year is a direct input to any lender's view of the Council's debt position.
findings.quote: Year-end borrowings1,218,836 1,168,786

findings.headline: Council reversed its decision to fund certain capital spending from surplus HRA reserves, to meet a temporary accommodation rent overcharging provision
findings.detail: The paper says the reversal preserves HRA reserves but increases future borrowing to fund the associated capital expenditure. It says this is likely to increase HRA interest charges. The paper does not state the size of the provision.
findings.matters: Replacing reserve-funded capital with borrowing, to cover a rent overcharging provision, changes the HRA's debt profile and interest costs.
findings.figures: Gross debt to CFR 0.62 : 1 (2025/26) against 0.63 : 1 (2024/25); year-end borrowings £1,218,836k against £1,168,786k
findings.quote: the council reversed its previous decision to fund certain capital expenditure from surplus HRA reserves

findings.headline: The medium-term funding gap for 2027/28 to 2029/30 moved from £80.9m in the February 2026 MTFS to £102m over the next three years
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase mainly to temporary accommodation pressures, particularly the rising cost of provision against budget, alongside continuing demand pressures. The Council plans to close the gap through transformation, savings, expenditure reductions and income generation. The 2026/27 budget is balanced.
findings.matters: A gap that rose from £80.9m to £102m within the same planning cycle, with no closing plan yet specified in the paper, is what lenders and peers will track in the next MTFS.
findings.figures: £80.9m cumulative gap 2027/28 to 2029/30 (February 2026 MTFS); £102m over the next three years (latest assessment)
findings.quote: identifying a £102m funding gap over the next three years

findings.headline: The overall General Fund balance fell by £33.2m during 2025/26, after an £11m decrease in 2024/25
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall to financial pressures and planned uses of reserves for investment in services. It says reserves continue to provide a buffer, but that reserve levels have reduced.
findings.matters: A fall of £33.2m in the General Fund balance in a single year shows how far reserves are being drawn down to meet a budget gap.
findings.figures: £33.2m fall in 2025/26; £11m decrease in 2024/25; usable reserves £497,744k (2025/26) against £503,438k (2024/25)
findings.quote: overall general fund balance fell by £33.2m during 2025/26

findings.headline: The General Fund recorded an adverse outturn of £25.3m in 2025/26, funded from reserves
findings.detail: The paper says the outturn is the monitoring and budgetary position and does not directly reconcile to the financial statements. It also says the separate provision for historic temporary accommodation rent overcharging is not part of this £25.3m. The paper links the outturn to temporary accommodation and social care pressures.
findings.matters: A General Fund overspend funded from reserves, with the reconciliation to the accounts explained, is a direct comparison point for other councils' outturn and reserve use.
findings.figures: £25.3m adverse outturn (budget monitoring basis); 2024/25 actual surplus/(deficit) excluding HRA of (5,325) in £'000
findings.quote: The General Fund recorded an adverse outturn of £25.3m which was funded from reserves.

findings.headline: The 2025/26 departmental savings schedule identified £15.8m of savings, with £9.4m rated green at year end
findings.detail: The paper says delivery was mixed, with £5m rated amber and £1.4m rated red. It attributes delays to certain transformational savings schemes, including slower mobilisation of implementation teams. The Council identified mitigating actions where savings were delayed or at risk.
findings.matters: It shows how much of a £15.8m savings schedule was on track at year end, and where delivery slipped, for a finance director comparing savings tracking with peers.
findings.figures: £15.8m savings identified; £9.4m (approximately 60%) rated green; £5m rated amber; £1.4m rated red
findings.quote: of which £9.4m, approximately 60%, was rated green, with £5m rated amber and £1.4m rated red.

findings.headline: Council's finance system implementation is currently planned to go live in April 2027, while over-privileged access on the legacy SAP system remains an open control issue.
findings.detail: The auditor found continued over-privileged access to SAP and said working practices are not in line with current best practice. The auditor notes the council is replacing SAP and does not expect significant improvement until the new system is in place.
findings.matters: A finance director running a legacy ERP through a replacement would want to see the timing for go-live and how the interim control gap is being managed.
findings.quote: The Finance implementation is currently planned to go live in April 2027.

findings.headline: Council made several self-identified changes to its draft accounts, including fixed asset valuations, before publication, and the auditor expects to sign its opinion on 27 November 2026.
findings.detail: The Council corrected its draft accounts for fixed asset valuations and other balances before the final version. The auditor recommends allowing more time for review and correction before the publication deadline, and the management response accepts this. Signing on 27 November 2026 is subject to approval of the statement of accounts and to the outstanding matters being resolved.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to see how the late corrections affected the publication timetable, especially for a large property portfolio.
findings.figures: £28,885k provision correction (corrected factual misstatement); £4,280k investment property correction; 27 November 2026 expected opinion date
findings.quote: following the publication of the draft financial statements

findings.headline: Auditor identified no significant weaknesses in the council's value-for-money arrangements for 2025/26, though its commentary is not yet final.
findings.detail: The auditor reports no significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, or improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Its commentary is not finalised because of work it is doing in response to an objection, and the outcome may have a material bearing on the commentary.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know whether the value-for-money conclusion is final before relying on it, given the open objection work.
findings.quote: We did not identify any significant weaknesses.

findings.headline: Auditor issued statutory recommendations under Section 27 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act on the council's major works response.
findings.detail: The auditor says some elements of the council's response are not adequate, including actions being closed without clear evidence of improvement. The recommendations are published in the Auditor's Annual Report. The council's own review found that procurement policies were not complied with and that conflicts of interest existed in the management of works contracts.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations are a formal escalation, and a finance director would want to see what triggered one and how the council has to respond.
findings.quote: we have considered it appropriate to issue statutory recommendations in accordance with Section 27 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act

findings.headline: Auditor was satisfied that arrangements to manage the major works scheme have been strengthened, under a significant value-for-money risk on major works.
findings.detail: The auditor had raised a significant value-for-money risk that improvements to major works governance might not have been implemented. It is satisfied that governance has been strengthened, but says it cannot guarantee that the works will be successful or keep to budget.
findings.matters: Other councils running major works programmes after comparable contract-management failures would want to see how the auditor tested whether governance changes were in place.
findings.quote: we were satisfied that arrangements to manage the major works scheme have been strengthened

findings.headline: Auditor found one investment property, a Old Kent Road asset let ahead of regeneration, valued £4m below market evidence, and the adjustment has been made.
findings.detail: The auditor concluded that the valuer had not appropriately considered market evidence that contradicted the value adopted. Owing to the unique nature of the asset and the regeneration programme, the auditor was satisfied the error was not more widespread. The adjustment is recorded in the corrected misstatements table.
findings.matters: A finance director holding regeneration-linked commercial property would want to know how interim lettings ahead of redevelopment are valued.
findings.figures: £4m understatement; £307.5m investment property portfolio (as at 31 March 2025); £4,280k corrected judgemental misstatement
findings.quote: the valuation was understated by £4m

findings.headline: Council adjusted its £3,563m dwellings valuation down by 4.2% to bridge from a 31 December 2025 valuation to 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: Cluttons' valuation was dated 31 December 2025 and was adjusted to the 31 March 2026 year end on the valuer's advice. The auditor considered the adjustment reasonable but said good practice would be to value at 31 March 2027. The auditor also flagged one large beacon in SE15 where the recorded increase conflicted with market data.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know how the year-end dwellings valuation was bridged from an earlier date, and whether the next revaluation will be aligned to the balance sheet date.
findings.figures: £3,563m dwellings balance; 4.2% downward adjustment; £3.5bn dwellings value at 31/3/25
findings.quote: the Council adjusted the valuation downwards by 4.2% as recommended by Cluttons

findings.headline: Council identified a £3.7m provision for over-charged rents to temporary accommodation tenants in HRA properties, with the revised liability totalling £34m.
findings.detail: The council found that temporary accommodation tenants in HRA properties had been over-charged since a 2020 Rent Standard change, which it did not act on at the time. Current tenants were refunded and the auditor agreed that the provision for former tenants and DWP-linked rents should also be recognised, with 25% of former tenants' rents provided for.
findings.matters: Any council that let HRA voids as temporary accommodation could face the same refund exposure if regulatory rent changes were not applied.
findings.figures: £3.7m provision relating to current tenants; £34m revised liability in total; 25% of rents linked to former tenants provided for
findings.quote: The Council identified a provision of £3.7m relating to these tenants

findings.headline: Council reversed its decision to fund council-home maintenance from surplus HRA reserves, so it will borrow for that capital spend instead, to help fund a temporary accommodation rent provision.
findings.detail: The temporary accommodation over-charging provision was funded by reversing a 2025 Executive decision to pay for maintenance and upgrades from surplus HRA reserves. The auditor notes the council will now borrow for that capital expenditure, which increases the Capital Financing Requirement and is likely to raise HRA interest charges in future years.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with an HRA would want to see how a rent-refund liability was funded by moving capital spend from reserves to borrowing, and what that does to HRA interest costs.
findings.figures: £3.7m provision for current tenants and DWP-linked rents; £34m revised liability in total; £28,885k provision correction in the audit misstatements table
findings.quote: To fund this provision the Council reversed a decision to meet the costs of maintaining and upgrading Council homes out of surplus HRA reserves

findings.headline: Planning materiality of £22.6m has been increased to £24.3m, using 31 March 2026 draft balances, with performance materiality moving from £16.9m to £18.2m
findings.detail: The audit plan was based on total assets at 31 March 2025. The auditor increased materiality using revised 31 March 2026 draft balances, and the reporting threshold stayed at £1.1m. No uncorrected or corrected misstatements were recorded.
findings.matters: A higher materiality threshold reflects the growth in the Fund's total assets, which a finance director at another fund can compare against their own asset base.
findings.figures: Materiality (1% of total assets) £22.6m planning, £24.3m final; performance materiality £16.9m to £18.2m; reporting threshold £1.1m
findings.quote: other than materiality. Materiality in the audit plan was based on total assets as per the 31 March 2025 audited accounts; however, it was increased using revised balances as per the 31 March 2026 draft accounts for audit.

findings.headline: Membership reconciliation recommendation is 'Partially Implemented', with discrepancies still found in active member records despite a reconciliation being provided during the year
findings.detail: The auditor found no formal annual membership reconciliation to validate movements against payroll data, and a number of discrepancies in active members. The Fund says it is strengthening the process during 2026/27, including employer-level pensioner membership analysis.
findings.matters: Membership data accuracy drives the liabilities used in triennial valuations, so a finance director at another fund will want to know whether the same reconciliation gap exists in their own records.
findings.figures: Status: 'Partially Implemented'; no figures on the number of discrepancies given
findings.quote: Although a reconciliation was provided during the year, a number of discrepancies were still identified in relation to active members.

findings.headline: Auditor found the review control over directly held property valuations ineffective for the second year, and management has closed the related recommendation without adopting it
findings.detail: The auditor found no management review control meeting auditing standards over the valuation of directly held property, which the Fund holds through Nuveen and values through Knight Frank. Management says its approach adequately addresses the risk, so the recommendation is recorded as closed.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of the same control finding, with management closing the recommendation, is a point of contention between audit and management that other pension funds' officers may face with their own auditors.
findings.figures: Directly held property c£268.9m at 31 March 2026 and c£248.3m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Consequently, this recommendation is outstanding but closed.

findings.headline: Journal entries in the Pension Fund's SAP ledger are not system-enforced for authorisation, and the recommendation to add an approval workflow is recorded as outstanding and not re-raised
findings.detail: Journal entries are authorised before posting by policy, but the SAP configuration does not enforce this. The auditor did not re-raise the recommendation because the Fund is migrating to a new SAP version and the replacement system is imminent.
findings.matters: A control gap where a journal can be posted without approval is a governance point that finance directors elsewhere will recognise, especially where a system change is used as the reason for not addressing it.
findings.figures: Recommendation status: 'Outstanding'; 1 significant control deficiency identified in the current year
findings.quote: the system – as configured – does not enforce authorisation meaning there is a risk that a journal could be posted without approval.

findings.headline: KPMG's audit scale fee for 2025/26 is £89,000 plus VAT, up from £86,000 in 2024/25, with fee variations for membership data and the triennial valuation still to be agreed
findings.detail: The PSAA scale fee rose from £86,000 to £89,000 plus VAT. The auditor says proposed fee variations for additional work on membership data and the triennial valuation are at the time of writing and the amount is shown as 'TBC'.
findings.matters: Additional audit work tied to membership data and the triennial valuation is a cost pressure that other funds' finance teams may see in their own audit fee variations.
findings.figures: 2025/26 scale fee £89.0k (£89,000 plus VAT); 2024/25 £86.0k; variations 'TBC'
findings.quote: proposed fee variations for 25-26 relate to additional work required over membership data and the pension fund triennial valuation.

findings.headline: KPMG expects to issue an unmodified auditor's report on the Pension Fund's 2025/26 financial statements, with sign-off on 30 November 2026 subject to outstanding matters
findings.detail: The report says the audit is substantially complete, with four outstanding items including review of updated draft accounts and receipt of the signed letter of representation. The auditor reports no modifications and no significant difficulties during the audit.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, can see the audit opinion status and the specific steps still open before the Fund's accounts are signed.
findings.figures: Sign-off expected 30 November 2026; scale fee £89,000 plus VAT
findings.quote: We expect to issue an unmodified Auditor’s Report.

findings.headline: KPMG expects to issue its audit opinion and final value for money conclusions by the end of November 2026, subject to completing its final procedures.
findings.detail: The auditor is completing final procedures on the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts. The paper gives end of November 2026 as the expected date for the audit opinion and final value for money conclusions, conditional on satisfactory completion of that work.
findings.matters: The sign-off date sets when the council's 2025-26 audited position becomes available to lenders and to peers comparing their own timetables.
findings.quote: Subject to satisfactory completion of this work, the auditor expects to issue its audit opinion and final Value for Money conclusions by the end of November 2026

findings.headline: The draft Auditor's Annual Report recognises improvements in governance and oversight and identifies a small number of areas for further action.
findings.detail: The paper says the report recognises improvements in governance and oversight. It also identifies a small number of areas where further action and continued monitoring are required, which the council says it is progressing through established governance arrangements.
findings.matters: Auditor-recognised governance improvements, alongside named areas still open, give peers a concrete reference for the governance changes Southwark has made.
findings.quote: The report recognises improvements in governance and oversight while identifying a small number of areas where further action and continued monitoring are required.

findings.headline: KPMG's draft Auditor's Annual Report reports no significant weaknesses in Southwark's value for money arrangements for 2025-26.
findings.detail: The draft Auditor's Annual Report is described as giving an overall positive assessment for 2025/26. It pairs an unmodified audit opinion with no significant weaknesses identified in value for money arrangements.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council, or a lender, can use the value for money conclusion as a direct comparison point for governance and resource use.
findings.quote: The draft Auditor’s Annual Report provides an overall positive assessment for 2025/26, with an unmodified audit opinion and no significant weaknesses identified in the Council’s value for money arrangements.

findings.headline: KPMG expects to issue an unmodified audit opinion on Southwark's 2025-26 financial statements, with management having agreed actions on the auditor's recommendations.
findings.detail: The ISA 260 report summarises agreed audit adjustments and recommendations from the review of financial and IT controls. The auditor expects an unmodified opinion, and the paper says management has agreed actions to address the recommendations.
findings.matters: An unmodified opinion with agreed control recommendations is the baseline a finance director would compare their own year-end against.
findings.quote: The auditor expects to issue an unmodified audit opinion, and management has agreed appropriate actions to address the recommendations

findings.headline: KPMG has issued the final audit completion certificate for Southwark's 2024-25 accounts after completing its work on an objection.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the auditor's work on an objection relating to the 2024-25 accounts is complete. The final audit completion certificate has been issued.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can see that a public objection to a prior-year set of accounts has been closed with a completion certificate.
findings.quote: The auditor’s work on an objection in respect of 2024-25 accounts is now complete, and the final audit completion certificate has been issued by the auditor.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Statement of Accounts 2025-26 for Southwark Council and Pension Fund
findings.headline: Staff employed at 31 March 2026 totalled 5,186, against 5,385 at 31 March 2025.
findings.detail: The narrative report gives the workforce figure, including permanent and fixed-term staff, and records the prior year's figure for comparison.
findings.matters: Staff numbers that fall by 199 in a year, while demand pressures rise, are a workforce change a finance director would want to compare against their own establishment.
findings.figures: 5,186 staff (31 March 2026); 5,385 staff (31 March 2025)
findings.quote: a total of 5,186 staff were employed as at 31 March 2026, including permanent and fixed-term staff, (5,385 as at 31 March 2025)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Statement of Accounts 2025-26 for Southwark Council and Pension Fund
findings.headline: The auditor has "nothing to report" on significant weaknesses in arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the use of resources.
findings.detail: Under the NAO Code of Audit Practice, the auditor reports only where it identifies significant weaknesses in arrangements. The paper states it has nothing to report in this respect, and nothing to report on the statutory reporting matters.

findings.matters: A rule that overruns and delays must go back to approval, rather than being absorbed as routine monitoring, is a control finance directors at other councils may be looking to adopt or compare with.

findings.headline: The council is committed to making future payments to cover its pension deficit, with the revenue implications built into the MTFS

findings.quote: The Council will not borrow to invest primarily for financial return.

findings.matters: Housing investment on this scale is a major call on capital resources, and lenders and finance directors will want to know how it is funded and governed.

findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement was forecast at £2,246m for 2025-26 but actual closing CFR was £1,962m. This significant £284m variance reflects either overly conservative planning or capital programme slippage. The undershoot affected planned borrowing drawdown, and the council ended with higher cash reserves than forecast, reducing the need for external borrowing.

findings.detail: The HRA's ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream was forecast at 15% but actual outturn was 44%, a deterioration of 29 percentage points. This means the HRA is now spending significantly more of its revenue on debt service than anticipated, materially reducing the revenue available for service delivery and housing investment. The General Fund similarly deteriorated from 8% forecast to 15% actual, though less severely.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the HRA's revenue is being consumed by financing costs at nearly triple the forecast rate, which materially affects HRA financial sustainability and its capacity to deliver services and manage debt repayment.

Peer benchmarking shows 0% probability of default and returns in the top quartile of comparable councils. This reflects effective treasury execution and sound counterparty selection.

The modest net increase reflects that the council simultaneously expanded its investment holdings (from £53m to £98m), offsetting much of the new borrowing. This indicates prudent cash management and suggests the council is holding higher liquid reserves.
findings.matters: A lender watches net debt growth as a sign of leverage. A 0.3% increase despite active capital investment signals disciplined borrowing and potentially strong cash generation or reserve accumulation.

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision increased 29% from £40.0m to £51.6m, reflecting growth in the capital financing requirement.
findings.detail: The increase is driven by expanded capital spending (and IFRS 16 lease accounting). This is the council's annual charge to repay debt from revenue, and the £11.6m increase represents cash that must be set aside each year going forward, reducing resources available for service delivery.
findings.matters: MRP is a binding annual obligation from debt already incurred. A sharp rise signals higher debt-serving costs going forward and constrains future borrowing capacity. Lenders track this as an indicator of debt sustainability.
findings.quote: The 2025/26 MRP charge increased from £40.0m in 2024/25 to £51.6m in 2025/26, primarily due to an increase in the Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) and IFRS16 lease accounting

This is refinancing and liquidity event reflecting the council's active debt management.
findings.matters: A lender tracks refinancing decisions and rates as measures of borrowing cost and rollover risk. The 5.42% rate in a rising-rate environment is material to the council's future debt service and affordability.

findings.paper_title: Report: Policy and Resources: Capital Monitoring report Month 4, 2026-27
findings.headline: The ten-year General Fund capital forecast shows minimal approved investment beyond 2028-29, creating uncertainty about future capital needs and debt trajectory.
findings.detail: Several discrete grant-funded schemes (Highshore SEND expansion, Beormund Primary relocation) are expected to complete within the next few years. The council explicitly states the forecast reduction from 2028-29 onwards reflects lack of approved capital priorities for years four to ten, not reduced investment need. Multiple rolling programmes (tree planting ~£1.5m p.a., DFG adaptations, Building Compliance) are expected to continue but only the next two years are loaded into the forecast.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the published ten-year forecast may understate true investment needs, affecting the council's likely future debt trajectory and capital borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Years 4-10 investment significantly lower than years 1-3; multiple rolling programmes expected to continue beyond current forecast
findings.quote: Beyond that point, the forecast reduces not because investment needs stop, but because the council has not yet identified or approved its capital priorities for years four to ten of the programme.

findings.paper_title: Report: Policy and Resources: Capital Monitoring report Month 4, 2026-27
findings.headline: £70m of General Fund capital spend slipped between the Month 4 forecast and year-end outturn in 2025-26, indicating programme delivery risk.

findings.matters: A lender assesses the reliability of capital forecasts and the council's ability to deliver programmes on schedule; significant slippage can extend debt maturity and delay benefit realisation.

findings.quote: In 2025-26, £70m of General Fund spend slipped between the forecast reported at M04 and the year-end outturn position.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme requires £221m of prudential borrowing (62% of the £356m ten-year programme), with concentration in the first two years as grant-funded schemes complete.

findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the housing investment programme may be materially reshaped, affecting future debt requirements and the affordability of the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Report: Policy and Resources: Capital Monitoring report Month 4, 2026-27
findings.headline: Interest rates on new borrowing are expected to remain elevated, with PWLB rates reflecting geopolitical conflict and persistent UK inflation.

PWLB rates remain elevated due to ongoing geopolitical conflict, international trade uncertainty and persistently high UK inflation, which keeps government bond yields high.
findings.matters: A lender assesses debt cost risk; elevated long-term rates increase the council's debt service burden and reduce flexibility to refinance or take new borrowing.

findings.quote: Interest rates on new borrowing are expected to remain higher than those experienced in recent years, increasing the cost of servicing new debt over the long term. PWLB borrowing rates also remain elevated, reflecting ongoing geopolitical conflict, international trade uncertainty and persistently high UK inflation.

findings.paper_title: Report: Policy and Resources: Capital Monitoring report Month 4, 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA borrowing of approximately £480m over the planning period is forecast to generate revenue costs of around £23.9m per annum at current 5% interest rates.
findings.detail: The Housing Investment Programme requires £479.7m total borrowing to be fully delivered over the remaining term. At long-term borrowing rates of approximately 5%, this translates to approximately £23.9m in annual borrowing costs, creating ongoing pressure on the HRA revenue budget alongside the existing Minimum Revenue Provision charge.
findings.matters: A lender assesses the affordability of debt service; HRA revenue pressure from housing borrowing affects the council's ability to sustain rental income and service existing debt.
findings.figures: £479.7m HRA borrowing requirement; £23.9m per annum borrowing costs at 5%
findings.quote: it includes forecast borrowing of approximately £480m over the planning period. This could generate borrowing costs of around £23.9m per annum when fully financed at current long-term borrowing assumptions of approximately 5%.

findings.paper_title: Report: Policy and Resources: Capital Monitoring report Month 4, 2026-27
findings.headline: A historic Temporary Accommodation rent methodology error required a £19.2m accounting adjustment and increase to HRA borrowing to maintain programme funding.
findings.detail: The council's closure of 2025-26 accounts identified that rent-setting methodology for TA properties in the HRA had not fully reflected statutory requirements. The council revised the accounting treatment and increased the provision for potential historic liability, redirecting £19.2m from revenue contributions to strengthen the provision, offset by equivalent increase in HRA borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether other material accounting adjustments may emerge from the HRA, and whether the increased borrowing requirement affects debt affordability.
findings.figures: £19.2m CERA redirected; £19.2m increase in HRA borrowing
findings.quote: the methodology applied in previous years did not fully reflect the rent setting requirements applicable to these properties. As a result, the council has revised its accounting treatment and increased the provision for the potential historic liability associated with refunding rents.

findings.paper_title: Report: Policy and Resources: Capital Monitoring report Month 4, 2026-27
findings.headline: Government-retained Right-to-Buy receipts are now conditional on spending within agreed deadlines, with repayment required for unspent amounts.
findings.detail: The council has approval to retain previously unspent RtB receipts, reducing the risk of loss to government. However, MHCLG will monitor progress and any failure to meet agreed expenditure deadlines could result in the receipts becoming repayable. This creates a new funding constraint that is driving the £424.3m programme increase.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the conditional nature of this funding source and the risk that capital programmes dependent on it could face repayment if deadlines are missed.
findings.figures: £424.3m programme increase; £281.0m Right to Buy Buyback Programme (2025-31); £59.5m of identified RtB receipts identified
findings.quote: This provides greater certainty over a funding source that would otherwise have been returned to Government. However, it also creates a requirement for the council to ensure that retained receipts are applied to eligible housing projects within the agreed timescales. Progress will be monitored by MHCLG, and any failure to meet the agreed deadlines could result in the receipts becoming repayable.

findings.headline: £1,000k adult social care efficiency depends on promoting client independence, marked amber for delivery risk

findings.detail: A significant income target of £1,000k from 'Rental Income generation from Tooley Street' (ref 217) is marked RED, suggesting the council itself is uncertain whether this income will be delivered.
